instruction: Please implement a website for a credit repair company to generate leads. The website should have a form-filling function, allowing users to input personal information and credit status. The website should also have a credit score inquiry function and an introduction to credit repair services. Users can browse the website, learn about credit repair services, and fill out the form to submit lead information. Set old lace as the body background and use rosy brown for the UI.

ui_instruct.task: Test the form submission functionality by inputting valid personal information and credit status details.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The form should submit successfully without errors, and a confirmation message should display indicating the lead information was recorded.

ui_instruct.task: Verify the credit score inquiry function by accessing the feature and submitting a valid input.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The system should process the inquiry without errors and provide appropriate feedback or next steps for the user regarding their credit score.

ui_instruct.task: Ensure content accuracy by reviewing the informational text on credit repair services presented on the homepage.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The content should be relevant, free of grammatical errors, and provide a clear introduction and explanation of the credit repair services offered by the company.

ui_instruct.task: Check and navigate to an introduction to credit repair services.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website shows an introduction to credit repair services.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'old lace' as the background color and 'rosy brown' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'old lace' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'rosy brown', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.instruction: People who run the credit score inquiry always ask the same thing next — okay, but how much could it actually go up? Give me a Score Improvement Estimator page: they type a current score (only accept 300 through 850) plus how many collections, late payments, and hard inquiries they've got, and the projected score recalculates live as they type — +25 points per collection we'd remove, +15 per late payment, +5 per inquiry, but never past 850 — then it recommends a plan off the total gain: under 40 points is Basic, 40 to 75 is Standard, over 75 is Premium. Wire it into the credit score inquiry you already built: after someone submits an inquiry, offer a 'project my improvement' button that opens the estimator with their score carried over (add a current-score field to the inquiry if it doesn't already ask for one). And two house rules for everything in this app from here on out, including whatever we add later: any credit score shown anywhere gets its band right next to it — under 580 Poor, 580-669 Fair, 670-739 Good, 740-799 Very Good, 800 and up Excellent, like '612 (Fair)' — and every form or tool keeps a visible 'Start over' that wipes it back to a fresh blank state.
follow_ups.source_feature: Free credit assessment CTA with multi-step intake form

ui_instruct.task: Open the Score Improvement Estimator, type 820 as the current score, and type 3 into the collections field, leaving late payments and hard inquiries at 0.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The projected score displays as 850 (Excellent) — capped at the maximum — not 895.

ui_instruct.task: On the Score Improvement Estimator, type 545 as the current score, then type 2 into the collections field, without clicking any calculate or submit button.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The projection updates by itself as values are typed: the current score is shown as 545 (Poor) and the projected score as 595 (Fair).

ui_instruct.task: On the Score Improvement Estimator, enter 600 as the current score, 1 collection, and 1 late payment.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The projected score reads 640 (Fair) and the recommended plan is Standard — the 40-point gain falls in the 40-75 range, not in Basic.

ui_instruct.task: Submit a credit score inquiry entering 640 as the current score along with any other required details, then click the 'project my improvement' option it offers.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The Score Improvement Estimator opens with 640 already filled in as the current score, displayed as 640 (Fair).

ui_instruct.task: Fill out the lead form with valid personal information and credit status details and submit it.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The form submits successfully and a confirmation message appears indicating the lead information was recorded.

follow_ups.instruction: Time for a Client Success Stories page to build trust. Start it with exactly these seven, I'll add more later: Marcus from Atlanta, Premium plan, 6 months, 5 stars, went 541 to 625; Denise from Tampa, Standard, 9 months, 4 stars, 588 to 655; Priya from Austin, Premium, 4 months, 5 stars, 612 to 679; Walter from Cleveland, Basic, 3 months, 3 stars, 601 to 639; Sofia from Phoenix, Premium, 12 months, 5 stars, 559 to 671; James from Baltimore, Standard, 7 months, 4 stars, 566 to 621; and Keisha from Memphis, Basic, 5 months, 4 stars, 597 to 626. Visitors should be able to filter by plan and by typing a minimum points gained, and sort by biggest gain — when two people gained the same, the one with the shorter program takes the higher spot. Always show the average gain for whichever stories are currently visible, to one decimal place. One more thing that applies everywhere in this app from now on, including anything we add later: score gains always read like '+84 pts', plus sign and all.
follow_ups.source_feature: Client testimonials carousel with score improvements

ui_instruct.expected_result: The list starts Sofia (+112 pts), Marcus (+84 pts), then Priya (+67 pts) ahead of Denise (+67 pts) because Priya's 4-month program is shorter, and the average gain for the visible stories reads +64.6 pts — not +64 or +64.57.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Only Sofia, Marcus, and Priya remain visible, and the average gain updates to +87.7 pts.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Only the four stories with gains of 60 or more remain (Sofia, Marcus, Priya, Denise), and the average gain reads +82.5 pts.

follow_ups.instruction: Next: a Dispute Letter Builder page so visitors can draft their own bureau dispute letters. They pick a bureau (Equifax, Experian, or TransUnion), pick a reason — not my account, paid in full, incorrect balance, duplicate entry, or identity theft — then type the creditor name and account number, and the letter preview rebuilds itself as they type, ending in a copyable text block. Account numbers are digits only, 4 to 16 of them; anything else gets flagged with an error and no usable letter comes out. Stamp each valid letter with a reference code: the bureau prefix (EQ, EX, or TU), a dash, the first four letters of the creditor in caps, a dash, then the count of digits in the account number — so Equifax plus Capital One plus 44127788 comes out EQ-CAPI-8. One more thing: tie it back to the lead form on the home page — once somebody's submitted the lead form, the letter's signature line signs off with the name they gave there automatically, and until anyone has, it shows a '[Your Name]' placeholder in the signature spot.

ui_instruct.expected_result: A valid letter preview is produced whose reference code reads exactly EQ-CAPI-8.

follow_ups.instruction: Those letters shouldn't vanish after someone copies them — I want a Dispute Tracker. Put a 'save to my disputes' action on the letter builder that files the letter as a Draft case, and build a tracker page where every case moves Draft, then Sent, then Resolved, strictly in that order — no resolving something that was never sent — with each status group showing its cases. Preload five cases so it isn't empty: Midland Funding at TransUnion (Sent), LVNV Funding at Equifax (Sent), Portfolio Recovery at Experian (Draft), First Premier Bank at Equifax (Resolved), and Midland Funding again, this time at Equifax (Draft).
follow_ups.source_feature: Three-step visual process flow (Submit Info, We Analyze, We Dispute)

ui_instruct.expected_result: It contains exactly two cases: Midland Funding (TransUnion) and LVNV Funding (Equifax).

ui_instruct.expected_result: The case now appears under Resolved alongside First Premier Bank, the Sent group contains only LVNV Funding, and any displayed group tallies stay consistent with that (1 Sent, 2 Resolved).

follow_ups.instruction: Give me an Impact Dashboard page that brags about our numbers. From the success stories it should show clients helped, total points recovered, the average gain to one decimal — don't let it get rounded into a whole number — and a spotlight on the single best result with the client's name and city. Pull in the dispute side too: an 'items resolved' stat counting resolved cases in the tracker, and it has to move the moment another case gets resolved over there.

follow_ups.instruction: The site's looking patchy, so let's do a visual refresh applied identically everywhere — home page, the estimator, success stories, the letter builder, the dispute tracker, and the impact dashboard. Primary action buttons go saddle brown with white text, every page title gets centered, cards and panels get 12px rounded corners with a thin rosy brown border, and any status or plan badge becomes a pill shape with white text on rosy brown. Also add a centered footer tagline to every one of those pages: 'Rebuild. Restore. Rise.' No page keeps the old look — that's the whole point.

follow_ups.instruction: Let's actually let people sign up. Build an enrollment flow: first pick a plan — Basic $49.99/mo, Standard $89.99/mo, Premium $129.99/mo — with optional add-ons rush processing ($19.99/mo) and credit monitoring ($9.99/mo); then contact details, where they need a name and a real-looking email before moving on; then a review step showing the monthly total and the first payment, which adds a one-time $25.00 setup fee — except Premium, where we waive it. And wire in the estimator: its plan recommendation should carry an enroll button that lands here with that plan already selected.
follow_ups.source_feature: Online sign-up forms converting visitors into paying clients

follow_ups.instruction: The tracker tells clients where each case sits, but not what to actually do next — so add a Dispute Strategy Advisor page. It reads the tracker as it stands right now, never a stale snapshot, and rolls the cases up by creditor: Midland gets one card even though we're fighting them at two bureaus. Each creditor card works out the next move — if any of their cases is still a Draft, it says 'Send the pending letter'; otherwise if anything's Sent, 'Await the bureau's response'; and once everything with that creditor is Resolved, 'Request an updated credit report'. Rank the cards by a priority score shown on the card: 2 points for every case of theirs that isn't resolved yet, plus a 3-point bonus when we're disputing them at more than one bureau — tag those cards 'multi-bureau' — and break ties alphabetically by creditor name. Change a case over in the tracker and the advisor better show it the moment you come back.
follow_ups.source_feature: Automated dispute workflow with recommended next actions per creditor

target_app_summary: What began as an old-lace-and-rosy-brown lead-gen brochure site for a credit repair company has grown into a full client acquisition and service portal. Discovery and conversion now run through a live score-improvement estimator wired to the original credit score inquiry, a tie-aware filterable success-stories directory, and a checkout-style plan enrollment flow that inherits the estimator's plan recommendation. Service delivery grew its own arm rooted in the original lead form: the form's submitted name auto-signs the dispute letter builder's letters, saved letters feed a Draft/Sent/Resolved dispute tracker, and the tracker in turn drives both an impact dashboard and a per-creditor dispute strategy advisor that rolls cases up by creditor, ranks them by a priority score with a multi-bureau bonus, and derives each creditor's next move. A consultation scheduler with per-advisor slot availability and a site-wide brand restyle round it out. The feature graph has one deep service chain (lead form -> letter builder -> tracker -> dashboard/advisor), a conversion chain (inquiry -> estimator -> enrollment), and three silent app-wide conventions (score band labels, '+N pts' gain formatting, Start-over resets) tested across every new surface.

edges.what: inquiry's captured score prefills the estimator
lead form's submitted name auto-signs the generated dispute letters
saved letters become Draft dispute cases
aggregates the seven pinned success stories
items-resolved stat counts tracker's resolved cases live
restyles home page and lead form
restyles success stories page and plan badges
restyles dispute tracker and status badges
estimator's plan recommendation preselects the enrollment plan
advisor rolls live tracker cases into per-creditor next actions and priority rankings

global_rules.rule: Every displayed credit score carries its band label next to it — under 580 Poor, 580-669 Fair, 670-739 Good, 740-799 Very Good, 800+ Excellent — e.g. '612 (Fair)'.
Every form or tool surface keeps a visible 'Start over' control that resets it to its initial blank state.
Score gains always render with a leading plus sign and 'pts' suffix, e.g. '+84 pts'.
